item.content:encoded: Boston Dynamics, a humanoid robot maker owned by Hyundai Motor Group, said it had appointed Rohit Prasad as chief executive officer, effective October 7. Prasad previously served as senior vice president and head scientist for Alexa and Artificial General Intelligence at Amazon (AMZN.O) . Prasad will bring his experience turning physical AI breakthroughs into commercial success, Boston Dynamics said. He succeeds Robert Playter, who [USN:L4N3Z70HG TEXT:"stepped down"] in February. Hyundai Motor Group [USN:L1N3Y60XL TEXT:"said in January"] it aims to build a factory capable of manufacturing 30,000 robot units annually by 2028, when it plans to start deploying them across all of its manufacturing sites.

item.title: HSBC plans job cuts across UK wealth business in AI push, FT reports
item.description: HSBC is planning sweeping job cuts across its UK wealth management business, including a sharp reduction in financial advisers and specialist staff, as part of a broader push to integrate AI, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: HSBC (HSBA.L) is planning sweeping job cuts across its UK wealth management business, including a sharp reduction in financial advisers and specialist staff, as part of a broader push to integrate AI, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The bank plans to cut about half of management and specialist roles in the business, while reductions among financial advisers could reach around 70%, the report said, citing people familiar with the plans. HSBC does not disclose the number of employees in its UK wealth business, though it is thought to have hundreds of relationship managers across the country, according to the FT. The bank did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours. "HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider," the bank said in a statement to Reuters. "We're continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally enabled products and journeys to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers." The bank is currently in a consultation period on the proposed changes, the report said, adding that affected employees are expected to leave by the end of the month. In May, Chief Executive Georges Elhedery [USN:L1N41X017 TEXT:"said"] at an HSBC investor day event that staff needed to embrace AI-driven change rather than resist it and that "generative AI will destroy certain jobs". Elhedery has made AI a central part of his strategy since taking over in 2024, deploying the technology across multiple functions and businesses to simplify operations and personalize content for customers. Banks across the globe have increased investments in AI, reshaping workforces and leading to changes in job roles. This has deepened concerns among economists that AI will upend established industries, with job losses already emerging in sectors most exposed to automation.

item.title: African Union to launch continent's first credit rating agency
item.description: The African Union will launch the continent's first credit rating agency on Wednesday, seeking to provide an alternative to the "big three" global ratings agencies as debt burdens weigh on many African economies.
item.dc:creator: Duncan Miriri
item.content:encoded: The African Union will launch the continent's first credit rating agency on Wednesday, seeking to provide an alternative to the "big three" global ratings agencies as debt burdens weigh on many African economies. The launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency will take place in Port Louis, capital of Mauritius, where the agency will be based. The project has been nearly a decade in the making, with African leaders endorsing its creation in 2018. "AfCRA complements existing global credit rating agencies by offering a perspective rooted in African data, expertise and realities," the African Union said in a statement. African leaders have long accused Western ratings agencies of failing to fairly assess the risk of lending to African countries and of moving too quickly to downgrade them during crises such as conflicts and pandemics. The agencies reject that criticism, saying they apply the same methodologies globally. A 2024 Reuters investigation into Africa's debt crisis found no evidence of systemic bias in the sovereign ratings assigned to the region by the three major global credit rating agencies. BORROWING COSTS IN FOCUS AfCRA, which will rate sovereign borrowers, financial institutions and private companies, will operate independently and be funded through shareholder capital and its operations, according to the AU. The AU did not provide details about the shareholders. The AU says the agency should help improve African countries' access to capital markets and provide investors with more balanced and context-specific assessments of economies across the continent. The drive to improve borrowing terms for the continent has become more urgent following years of increased government borrowing, pushing some countries into debt distress in recent years. "The stakes are significant," the AU said, adding that the continent's annual external debt service surged to $163 billion in 2024, from $61 billion in 2010. In many countries, interest payments have exceeded the annual budgets for key social sectors such as health and education. "AfCRA aims to reduce such burdens by improving investor confidence and market transparency," it said, adding that the agency will also rate non-African entities where appropriate. The AU said the new agency is also expected to boost coverage, with 23 economies on the continent lacking a rating from the three big agencies.

item.title: Padres closer Mason Miller on paternity list, missed Game 3 vs. Brewers
item.description: San Diego's All-Star closer Mason Miller was placed on the postseason paternity list on Tuesday with the host Padres facing elimination in Game 3 against the Milwaukee Brewers in their National League Division Series.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: San Diego's All-Star closer Mason Miller was placed on the postseason paternity list on Tuesday with the host Padres facing elimination in Game 3 against the Milwaukee Brewers in their National League Division Series. The Padres found a way to keep their season going, beating the Brewers 4-3 as right-hander Michael King registered a six-out save after throwing 72 pitches as their Game 2 starter on Sunday. King gave up one hit and walked two to record the save. Major League Baseball announced the move, which allows Miller to be away from the team for a minimum of one day and a maximum of three days. Miller's wife, Jordan, went into labor on Tuesday afternoon to deliver their first child, the Padres said before the game. Left-hander Wandy Peralta will be on San Diego's active roster until he is replaced by Miller. Manager Craig Stammen said Miller had communicated with the team in the early afternoon, telling them he was monitoring the situation to determine if he would be available to the team. "He decided that he needed to stay with his wife," Stammen said after the game. "We knew sometime in the afternoon, but we wanted to give him enough time in case the baby comes really quick or it goes the other way, and he could come to the game. We gave him the opportunity. We waited until an hour and a half, an hour before the game time to make the final call." Left-hander Adrian Morejon, a likely candidate to fill the closer role for San Diego, was held out due to a shoulder issue. Stammen said Morejon had played catch and threw off the mound earlier in the day. Miller, 28, is 0-1 with a 6.75 ERA, three walks, and four strikeouts over 2 2/3 innings in two appearances this postseason. He took the loss in Game 2 despite needing only 12 pitches to retire host Milwaukee's Nos. 2, 3 and 4 hitters in the eighth inning. Miller, who routinely pitches only one inning per game, came back out for the ninth, walked three batters and gave up Jackson Chourio's game-winning single with two outs, resulting in a 4-3 setback. Game 4 is Wednesday night in San Diego. Game 5, if necessary, is Friday in Milwaukee. Miller was 5-2 in the regular season with a 1.67 ERA and tied for the National League with 38 saves and 57 games finished. He had 26 walks and 129 strikeouts in 70 innings over 66 games and was selected an All-Star for the second time, and the first with the Padres. Peralta, 35, was 3-3 in 65 regular-season games (five starts) with a 3.61 ERA, 23 walks and 50 strikeouts in 77 1/3 innings. The Padres also announced on Tuesday that first baseman Gavin Sheets was out of the starting lineup for Game 3 due to neck stiffness. He did not play in the game. San Diego also placed starting pitcher Walker Buehler on the postseason paternity list on Saturday. He was replaced by right-hander Randy Vasquez on the active roster before returning Monday. Buehler was 9-6 with a 4.63 ERA in 32 starts in his first season with the Padres. A two-time World Series champion with the Los Angeles Dodgers, Buehler did not pitch in the NL wild-card sweep against the Chicago Cubs. Game 1 of the NLDS would have been his turn in the starting rotation. --Field Level Media

item.title: Shares of Japan beer makers fall after raids over cartel suspicion
item.description: Japan's Fair Trade Commission said it raided the country's four major beer makers on suspicion of collusion in sales of beer and other products to wholesalers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Shares of major Japanese beer makers fell nearly 4% on Wednesday after Japan's Fair Trade Commission said it raided the country's four major beer makers on suspicion of collusion in sales of beer and other products to wholesalers. The beer divisions of Kirin Holdings Co (2503.T) , Asahi Group Holdings (2502.T) , unlisted Suntory Holdings as well as Sapporo Breweries (2501.T) , which together control more than 90% of Japan's domestic beer market, are suspected of coordinating prices over several years. Public broadcaster NHK said the Fair Trade Commission was probing whether the companies formed a cartel when they raised prices in April last year and October 2022, citing factors including rising raw material costs. The anti-trust watchdog is expected to continue its investigation and could file a criminal complaint, a source familiar with the matter said, declining to be named because the person was not authorised to talk to the press. The Commission declined to elaborate on the investigation. Shares in Sapporo fell as much as 3.73%, while Kirin briefly shed a little over 3% to hit its lowest level in more than three months. Asahi dropped nearly 2.5% before recouping some losses. In statements, the four beer makers separately confirmed the raids and said they intend to cooperate with the investigation. The Fair Trade Commission has carried out similar probes into well-known Japanese companies in recent months. In June, it raided six Japanese ice-cream makers, including Morinaga Milk Industry (2264.T) and Meiji Holdings (2269.T) , over allegations of operating a cartel.

item.title: Asia shares weaker, oil up as investors weigh Saudi-Houthi escalation
item.description: Asian markets were slightly weaker on Wednesday as investor confidence showed signs of flagging, while oil prices rose due to a storm threat in the Gulf of Mexico and escalating Saudi-Houthi tensions.
item.dc:creator: Scott Murdoch, Gregor Hunter
item.content:encoded: Asian markets were slightly weaker on Wednesday as investor confidence showed signs of flagging, while oil prices rose due to a storm threat in the Gulf of Mexico and escalating Saudi-Houthi tensions. In Asia, MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan (.MIAPJ0000PUS) was down 0.5%, led by declines in Hong Kong and Singapore after US stocks ended higher. The index is up 0.9% so far this month. The S&P 500 (.SPX) hit a fresh [USN:L6N45S16W TEXT:"record"] on Tuesday, up about 0.6% on the day, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq (.IXIC) gained 0.4%, also an all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 0.5%. In Asian trading, US crude ticked up 0.9% to $90.22 a barrel; prices were little changed in the international session. Brent crude rose 1% to $101.58 per barrel. The price rise came as commodity investors [USN:L4N45T01V TEXT:"weighed"] supply constraints from a storm heading for North American oil-producing regions and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia against increased supplies of Middle East crude. Around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products have left the Middle East on [USN:L6N45S0MD TEXT:"tankers"] in the last seven to 10 days, commodities trading giant Vitol's CEO Russell Hardy said on Tuesday. US equities were showing signs of losing momentum as global bond yields resumed their ascent on Wednesday. S&P 500 e-mini futures rose 0.1% for the fifth day of gains, but failed to surpass an intraday high set the previous session. Heavily sold French bond futures ticked down in Asia to retrace some of the previous session's [USN:L1N45N0A3 TEXT:"rebound"] as far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen [USN:L1N45S0C4 TEXT:"pledged"] spending cuts and a reduction in the country's budget deficit. Ten-year French yields fell more than 11 basis points on Tuesday and the spread between French OATs and German bunds , which hit almost 160 basis points last week, according to LSEG data, narrowed to 132 bps. "The magnitude of the move is striking given the 2027 election remains several months away and France's deteriorating fiscal dynamics are hardly new," said Laura Cooper, Nuveen's head of macro credit and global investment strategist. "What has changed is sharply higher yields, leaving investors less willing to look through those vulnerabilities." The resumption of investor concerns weighed on the euro , which slipped 0.3% to $1.1229. US TREASURY AUCTIONS TO SHOW DEPTH OF DEMAND The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 3.8 basis points at 5.307% in Asian trade ahead of an auction of notes of the same maturity later in the session and a 30-year auction on Thursday. The auctions will show the depth of investor demand for US debt, analysts said. US longer-dated yields hit a 24-year high on Monday amid a persistent selloff since late August due to inflation and debt concerns. Australian shares (.AXJO) were down 0.1% on Wednesday, while Japan's Nikkei stock index (.N225) was off 0.8%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index (.HSI) was down 0.5% in afternoon trading, dragged lower by a decline of as much as 4.1% in the city's biotech gauge (.HSBIO) . Mainland China's financial markets remained closed for a holiday. Indian stocks (.BSESN) slipped 0.5% as the Reserve Bank of India [USN:L1N45T036 TEXT:"hiked interest rates"] for the first time in nearly four years to rein in rising inflation. The central bank raised its benchmark by 25 basis points to 5.5%, as expected by a majority of economists polled by Reuters. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.1% to 102.06 following a 0.27% slide in the prior session. The Japanese yen weakened 0.2% to 158.41 per dollar. Sterling dipped 0.2% to $1.3248. The Federal Reserve on Wednesday will publish the minutes of its September 15 and 16 policy meeting, which will be scrutinised for potential rate moves over the next few months. Traders scaled back expectations of a Fed rate increase this month to 19% from about 50% a week earlier. Spot gold was down 0.6% at $4,137.29 per ounce.

item.title: Auston Matthews, Gavin McKenna hit milestones in Leafs' OT win
item.description: Auston Matthews scored with 14 seconds remaining in overtime as the Toronto Maple Leafs rallied from an early 3-0 deficit to defeat the visiting Nashville Predators 5-4 on Tuesday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Auston Matthews scored with 14 seconds remaining in overtime as the Toronto Maple Leafs rallied from an early 3-0 deficit to defeat the visiting Nashville Predators 5-4 on Tuesday night. Nashville goalie Juuse Saros made a skate save on a William Nylander shot, but the rebound slid to Matthews alone at the bottom of the right circle, where he fired a wrist shot inside the near post for the game-winner. Matthews, who also had three assists, passed Bill Guerin (429) into ninth place for most goals by United States-born skaters. Gavin McKenna, the first overall pick of the 2026 NHL Draft, scored his first career goal and also had his first assist for Toronto in the 18-year-old's first multi-point game in four outings. Nylander scored a goal and had two assists, Jack Roslovic had a goal and an assist, and John Tavares also scored for Toronto. Anthony Stolarz made 21 saves. Steven Stamkos and Nils Hoglander each scored two goals, Ryan O'Reilly picked up his 900th career point with an assist, and Filip Forsberg added two assists for Nashville. Stamkos moved into sole possession of 17th place on the NHL's all-time goal scoring list with his 626th and 627th career goals, breaking a tie with Joe Sakic and Jarome Iginla, who each scored 625. Saros finished with 32 saves for the Predators. Nashville, playing its first road game of the season, jumped out to a 2-0 lead in the first period on power-play goals. Stamkos snapped in a rebound of a Matthew Wood shot at the 7:13 mark, and Hoglander tucked in a rebound of an Adam Wilsby shot inside the left post at 9:08 of the first period. Hoglander made it 3-0 at the 3:03 mark of the second period when he slapped in a rebound from the right side of the net for his third goal in two games. Toronto got back into the game with two goals in a little over two minutes. Tavares started the comeback when he rushed down the left wing and fired a wrist shot bar down. McKenna picked up an assist on the score for his first NHL point. Nylander then, on a power play, buried a rebound of a Matthews shot from the slot for his third goal. Stamkos made it 4-2 with a wrist shot from the right circle, but Toronto answered just 61 seconds later on McKenna's first goal, a wrist shot from the right circle into the top far-left corner. The Maple Leafs tied it 4-4 midway through the third period when Roslovic, left alone at the bottom of the right circle, skated in and fired a wrist shot past Saros' glove side. Toronto appeared to take a 5-4 lead at the 11:49 mark when Nylander roofed a wrist shot from the right faceoff dot, but Nashville successfully challenged the play, determining that Nylander was offside entering the zone. --Field Level Media

item.title: Messi signs off in tears after one last Argentina master class
item.description: The 39-year-old's final bow in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental stadium was less about football and more a national celebration of Messi's service to the national team.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Lionel Messi delivered one last master class in blue and white on Tuesday as Argentina's captain brought the curtain down on his extraordinary 21-year international career by scoring one goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin. The 39-year-old's final bow in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental stadium was less about football and more a national celebration of Messi's service to the national team. Landmarks across the capital glowed with the team's sky blue and white colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans poured their hearts into a rendition of Argentina's national anthem. "It's hard to talk," said Messi, whose family watched proudly from the stands alongside some of Argentina's World Cup winners of 1978, 1986 and 2022. "There are a lot of emotions, a lot of things going through my head. The first thing I think about is my old man," he added, referring to the recent death of his father. "It was a huge source of pride for me to wear this shirt all this time, more than 20 years. "Not coming anymore is going to hurt a lot. I swear, I'd love to keep coming my whole life, because playing for Argentina is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you." 'GRACIAS' Hours earlier, a massive No. 10 shirt emblazoned with "Gracias" was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi's hometown. As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route. When the teams took the pitch, Benin's captain looked lost for words as he handed Messi a gift and letter during the pre-match handshake. After a goalless first half, Messi supplied the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home Argentina's opener. Otamendi shared 17 years with Messi in the national team, including four World Cups, and was also ending his international career. Messi then set up Nico Paz, one of the players seen as a potential successor for Argentina's No. 10 shirt, to score the second goal. In a fairytale ending, Messi converted a penalty for 3-0, his 126th international goal, prompting another round of "Messi, Messi" chants from the crowd. At the final whistle, teammates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky. Argentine singer Soledad Pastorutti, known as "La Sole", then sang her signature "Brindis" as part of a tribute to Messi and his journey with the national team. Messi leaves as the country's most-capped player (208) and record scorer having transformed years of frustration on the international stage into a story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs. For years, Argentina asked Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say 'Thank You'.

item.title: Indian shares trim losses after RBI rate hike as financials reverse declines
item.description: Indian shares trimmed losses on Wednesday as financial stocks reversed early declines after the RBI hiked rates by an expected 25 basis points and stayed away from additional measures to drain liquidity.
item.dc:creator: Bharath Rajeswaran
item.content:encoded: Indian shares trimmed losses on Wednesday as financial stocks reversed early declines after the RBI hiked rates by an expected 25 basis points and stayed away from additional measures to drain liquidity. The Reserve Bank of India increased its benchmark repo rate to 5.5%, its first hike since early 2023, and also changed its policy stance to "calibrated tightening" citing growth and inflation risks from higher oil prices and global monetary policy tightening. India's Nifty 50 (.NSEI) fell 0.44% to 22,677.35 and the Sensex (.BSESN) shed 0.25% to 72,887.99, as of 12:13 a.m. IST. The indexes had declined about 0.7% ahead of the rate decision. "A rate hike is not necessarily negative for banks: many private bank loans are directly linked to the repo rate, so lending rates reprice quickly," said Nirav Karkera, head of research and fund manager at W by Groww. "Private banks may see some near-term margin pressure from the large foreign currency deposit inflows, but this should ease as advances pick pace. PSU banks are better placed on margins near term," Karkera said. Financials (.NIFTYFIN) and banks (.NSEBANK) traded flat after the rate hike, erasing intraday losses of 0.5% and 0.7%, respectively, logged ahead of the policy decision. Private banks (.NIFPVTBNK) and state-owned banks (.NIFTYPSU) rose 0.2% and 1%, respectively. The lack of further liquidity-tightening measures also eased concerns over funding costs and near-term margin pressure, said two analysts. Twelve out of 16 major sectors logged losses. The broader small-caps (.NIFSMCP100) rose 0.6% and mid-caps (.NIFMDCP100) dropped 0.3%. Automobile (.NIFTYAUTO) , fast-moving consumer goods (.NIFTYFMCG) and real estate (.NIFTYREAL) lost 1.5%, 0.8% and 1%, respectively. Shares of Titan (TITN.NS) [USN:L4N45T073 TEXT:"fell"] about 4%, with analysts flagging weaker-than-expected growth in the firm's jewellery segment. Brent crude rose about 0.8% to $101.4 as storm risks to US oil output and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia outweighed increased Middle East supply.

item.title: Gold slips as dollar gains; investors await Fed minutes for rate clues
item.description: Gold prices slipped on Wednesday as the US dollar strengthened, while investors awaited minutes from the Federal Reserve's September meeting for clues on whether policymakers remain inclined to raise rates further.
item.dc:creator: Ashitha Shivaprasad
item.content:encoded: Gold prices slipped on Wednesday as the US dollar strengthened, while investors awaited minutes from the Federal Reserve's September meeting for clues on whether policymakers remain inclined to raise rates further. Spot gold fell 0.8% to $4,130.37 per ounce by 0627 GMT. US gold futures dropped 0.7% to $4,157.00. The US dollar index (.DXY) rose 0.3%, making greenback-priced metals more expensive for investors holding other currencies. Minutes of the latest Federal Open Market Committee meeting are due later in the day. "The yellow metal is likely to remain relatively stable with a mild downside bias," said Frank Walbaum, a market analyst at Naga.com. "Minutes will clarify the Fed's monetary policy and the degree of support among policymakers for further rate increases and could reshape upcoming hike odds. Subsequent moves in long-term Treasury yields, the dollar, or oil prices triggered by any Middle East developments would then amplify the directional impact (on gold)," Walbaum said. Recent comments from Fed officials underscored the US central bank's commitment to bringing inflation under control. San Francisco Fed President [USN:L6N45S13A TEXT:"Mary Daly"] said whether further rate hikes are needed depends largely on if the factors pushing up inflation fade or persist, while Kansas City Fed President [USN:S0N3XI00P TEXT:"Jeff Schmid"] said rates still need to rise further to bring inflation down. While recent soft economic data have dampened expectations of an October rate increase, traders are still pricing in an 88% chance of a hike by December, according to the CME's FedWatch tool. In a high-interest-rate environment, investors tend to favour yield-generating assets over gold. Separately, delegates attending the [USN:L1N45S0R9 TEXT:"London Bullion Market Association's"] annual conference in Sorrento, Italy, forecast that gold could reach $5,013 an ounce over the next 12 months. [USN:L1N45T01W TEXT:"China's central bank"] stepped up its gold purchases in September, extending its buying streak to a 23rd consecutive month, official data showed. Spot silver fell 1.9% to $60.54, platinum eased 1.3% to $1,679.20, and palladium lost 1.5% to $1,154.35.

item.title: Fresh wave of Russian attacks on Ukraine kills two in Kyiv
item.description: Two bodies were found as the air strike sparked a fire in a garage cooperative, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Two people were killed in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Wednesday, in the latest of Russia's near daily round-the-clock attacks on its neighbour in their fifth year of war, which also damaged city buildings and warehouses. Two bodies were found as the air strike sparked a fire in a garage cooperative, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. Blasts were heard in the city, a Reuters witness said. Separate air strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro have damaged an industrial facility, transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and apartment buildings in Kremenchuk, regional officials said on the Telegram messaging app.

item.title: Indonesia's Constitutional Court dismisses challenge to vice president over education credentials
item.description: Indonesia's Constitutional Court has ruled that incomplete education documents submitted by Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka before the 2024 election did not disqualify him from office, saying that questions about his eligibility were the responsibility of other institutions.
item.dc:creator: Ananda Teresia
item.content:encoded: Indonesia's Constitutional Court has ruled that incomplete education documents submitted by Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka before the 2024 election did not disqualify him from office, saying that questions about his eligibility were the responsibility of other institutions. Petitioners in the [USN:L6N45O0CD TEXT:"case"] against Gibran, the son of former President Joko Widodo, had argued that his foreign senior high school credentials did not meet legal requirements for vice-presidential candidates and were improperly accepted by election officials. All nine judges dismissed the petition, Chief Justice Suhartoyo said in a ruling issued late on Tuesday. Judge Adies Kadir said the court did not disqualify Gibran because the petition could no longer be treated as a dispute over the election result, as he had been sworn into office as vice president under President Prabowo Subianto. "Although the court found no convincing evidence that Gibran has a foreign diploma equivalent to having completed senior high school, or another equivalent school as stipulated in Election Law, the court cannot annul or disqualify him as requested by the petitioners," Adies said. Indonesia's election law requires presidential and vice-presidential candidates to have completed senior high school or hold an equivalent qualification. No graduation certificate was presented during the case, the ruling said. Responding to the court ruling, Gibran told reporters on Wednesday that he respected the court's processes and would continue working to ensure the success of Prabowo's programmes. Gibran attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore and UTS Insearch in Australia, before earning a bachelor's degree through the Management Development Institute of Singapore. "Well, if I had not graduated from high school, I would not have been able to go to college. I completed my bachelor's degree in Singapore," Gibran said. Adies said the court also found that the issue of Gibran's eligibility to serve as vice president fell under the authority of other institutions, without providing further details. Bambang Widjojanto, the petitioners' lawyer, said the ruling could provide grounds for parliament to impeach Gibran and stop him from standing in the next election unless he completed a government high school equivalency programme. In 2023, [USN:P8N3AJ004 TEXT:"the Constitutional Court"] sparked outrage after a ruling enabled Gibran to stand as vice president despite not meeting the 40-year age requirement.

item.title: Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies in Yemen
item.description: One missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land.
item.dc:creator: Enas Alashray, Mohammed Ghobari
item.content:encoded: Houthis attacked the international airport in the southern Yemeni town of Aden with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones early on Wednesday, Yemen's Transport Ministry said, as fighting [USN:L8N45M1W0 TEXT:"intensified"] across several fronts between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-led coalition, pushing to retake strategic territory seized by the Houthis, said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. The escalation came after Yemeni government forces, with Saudi-led coalition air support, launched a lightning counter-offensive this week to capture the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait shipping route and the city of Mocha. Yemen's government said that forced the Houthis out of areas they had captured last month, reviving a [USN:L6N45S0PX TEXT:"complex 12-year war,"] which led to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises and fragmented the Arab world's most impoverished country. One missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis. Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control. The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport. The Houthis, which control much of Yemen's north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran's influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement, with a spillover from the [USN:L6N45T01N TEXT:"Iran conflict"] triggering the latest fighting. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran's Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported. In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. It was not immediately clear whether this was linked to the missile the coalition said it had intercepted near Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

item.title: Dollar recoups losses as markets await Fed minutes, speakers
item.description: The US dollar recouped some losses on Wednesday as eyes turned to the release of Federal Reserve minutes and speeches by its policymakers for signals on a potential rate hike.
item.dc:creator: Rocky Swift
item.content:encoded: The US dollar recouped some losses on Wednesday as eyes turned to the release of Federal Reserve minutes and speeches by its policymakers for signals on a potential rate hike. The euro gave back some of its gains in the prior session when French bonds rallied after the frontrunner in next spring's presidential election outlined plans to slash spending. The yen weakened even after a dovish Bank of Japan board member said she would support interest rate increases. Later on Wednesday, the US central bank is due to release minutes of its September policy meeting when it raised interest rates to contend with inflation. Comments from Fed policymakers have come across as less hawkish following lower-than-expected personal consumption expenditure (PCE) data and jobs figures last week. "There seems to be a little bit less urgency on the Fed to hike rates after the softer PCE and then the nonfarm payroll reports recently," Gavin Friend, a senior markets strategist at National Australia Bank, said on a podcast. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.16% to 102.07, recovering from a 0.27% slide on Tuesday. The euro fell 0.25% to $1.123. The Japanese yen weakened 0.19% to 158.39 per dollar, and sterling lost 0.21% to $1.3244. The greenback also benefited from safe-haven demand after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Aden International Airport. To end a war that's roiled energy markets and stoked inflation for eight months, Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity, US Vice President JD Vance [USN:L6N45T01N TEXT:"told"] Reuters. Bond yields around the world have climbed in recent weeks due to expectations of central bank rate hikes as well as concerns about government finances. French debt is [USN:L6N45O0HP TEXT:"under growing pressure"] as politicians struggle to curb the budget deficit ahead of a divisive election in 2027. The calling of a [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"snap election in Spain"] added to the recent stress on the euro. The euro rallied sharply on Tuesday after far-right French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen raised her target for [USN:L1N45S0C4 TEXT:"spending cuts"] to €140 billion ($158 billion) from €125 billion in savings originally planned if she wins power in 2027. The Bank of Japan's new policymaker Ayano Sato said in an interview with the Kyodo news agency that she supports the idea of raising interest rates in several stages. The BOJ [USN:L4N45S011 TEXT:"may signal"] this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2% target, three people familiar with its thinking said, highlighting its readiness to raise interest rates again. OCTOBER FED HIKE EXPECTATIONS RETREAT Expectations for a Fed rate hike later this month have retreated but markets are still anticipating more increases later in the year and next year. In contrast to the recent call for patience from some Fed officials, Kansas City Fed President [USN:S0N3XI00P TEXT:"Jeff Schmid"] said on Tuesday that the central bank still needs to raise its policy rate further to lower inflation, even if higher long-term yields are weighing on activity in some parts of the economy. The chance of a hike of at least 25 basis points in October stands at 20.5%, from about 51% a week ago, according to CME FedWatch , but markets are pricing in an 84.5% chance of a hike at the December meeting. "With little forward guidance from Chair (Kevin) Warsh, markets have reacted sharply to each US data release and policymaker speech," Commonwealth Bank of Australia currency strategist Samara Hammoud said in a report. "We expect the Fed to wait until December before hiking again." Fed officials Christopher Waller, Neel Kashkari and Alberto Musalem are all due to speak later on Wednesday. The central bank is also scheduled to release consumer credit data, which is expected to show a decrease to $15 billion in August from $18.06 billion in July. The Australian dollar weakened 0.14% versus the greenback to $0.6972, while New Zealand's kiwi sank 0.28% to $0.5605. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 1.76% to $84,115.47, and ether declined 3.3% to $2,609.57.

item.title: Oil gains as US storm and Houthi air strikes threaten supply
item.description: Oil prices climbed on Wednesday as the market weighed supply constraints from a storm heading for US oil-producing regions and attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia against increased supplies of Middle East crude.
item.dc:creator: Jeslyn Lerh
item.content:encoded: Oil prices climbed on Wednesday as the market weighed supply constraints from a storm heading for US oil-producing regions and attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia against increased supplies of Middle East crude. Brent futures rose 81 cents, or 0.8%, to $101.39 a barrel by 0635 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures gained 61 cents, or 0.7%, to $90.05 a barrel. US forecasters said on Tuesday a [USN:L1N45S12U TEXT:"storm forming in the Gulf of Mexico"] would become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days and would likely hit oil and gas producing facilities. The offshore areas in the Gulf in the storm's path produce 15% of US crude oil and 5% of the country's natural gas. KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said the storm was an "unwelcome complication for crude, raising the prospect of production and refining disruptions at a time when the market already has enough supply-side headaches". The storm could affect six refineries. Refineries in US Gulf states account for about 50% of the national capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day (bpd). US crude oil inventories fell last week, market [USN:L6N45S1A7 TEXT:"sources said on Tuesday"], citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks fell by 2.09 million barrels in the week ended October 2. "For now, the market is likely to remain nervous to any potential supply disruptions," said ING commodity strategists, adding that supply risks from the Middle East are still very real amid continued attacks on ships. Supply has been recovering. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline hit 5.8 million barrels a day, the kingdom's energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, said on Tuesday. Around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products have left the Middle East on tankers in the last 7 to 10 days, [USN:L6N45S0MD TEXT:"the head of Vitol said"]. However, Saudi Arabia's airports in Jazan and Najran were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, [USN:L1N45S0BG TEXT:"the Saudi aviation authority said"], as hostilities between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis escalated. The attacks occurred as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pressed a major offensive to retake territory from the Houthis, after weeks of rebel advances, with Riyadh stepping up airstrikes in support of the campaign. Attacks and refinery outages are "likely to keep the cracks elevated and scarcity will transmit to crude," said Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at X Analysts in Sydney, referring to the premiums for refined products over crude. Crude prices would hold near $100 "without any material de-escalation emerging," he added. US-Iran relations are no closer to repair with US President Donald Trump [USN:L1N45S12U TEXT:"saying on Tuesday"] that nobody knew who was running Iran during the eight-month US-Israeli war with Iran.

item.title: Japan's $15 billion Rapidus chip bet hinges on winning customers
item.description: Japan's Rapidus, with $15 billion in state backing, is tying up with chip design firms as it seeks to answer a major question hanging over the country's tech ambitions: can a company with no manufacturing track record begin producing cutting-edge chips in a year?
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Okasaka, Sam Nussey
item.content:encoded: Japan's Rapidus, with $15 billion in state backing, is tying up with chip design firms as it seeks to answer a major question hanging over the country's tech ambitions: can a company with no manufacturing track record begin producing cutting-edge chips in a year? Only a handful of companies globally can make the 2-nanometre chips Rapidus wants to produce, which requires the industry's most advanced manufacturing technology. Chips produced with cutting-edge processes offer faster, more energy-efficient performance than earlier-generation chips. The leading companies are Taiwan's TSMC (2330.TW) , which spent decades refining its processes and dominates leading-edge chipmaking, South Korea's [USN:L1N41D03P TEXT:"Samsung"] Electronics (005930.KS) , which began producing 2-nm chips last year, and [USN:L6N3Y613X TEXT:"Intel"] (INTC.O) . The Rapidus venture, set up in 2022, must secure customers ahead of the planned launch of 2-nm chip production in the second half of the next fiscal year, a project that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is counting on to rebuild Japan's semiconductor industry. Rapidus said on Monday it would partner with 17 companies including US chip design software firm Synopsys (SNPS.O) and India's Infosys (INFY.NS) to help customers design chips, as the company seeks to secure manufacturing contracts. "The biggest question for Rapidus is still who will actually fill the fab," said Nori Chiou, investment director at White Oak Capital, using the industry terminology for a semiconductor fabrication plant. Rapidus' plant will be based in Hokkaido. While Monday's announcement was not yet evidence of commercial traction, he said, it represented incremental progress. Failure of the project would be a major setback for Japan's industrial strategy and could reverberate across the country's chip sector, as it seeks to strengthen supply chain resilience amid rising regional tensions and concerns over a possible Chinese move against Taiwan that could disrupt global supplies. HEAVYWEIGHT COMPETITION The unprecedented AI investment boom has fuelled demand for semiconductors and computing infrastructure, a trend Rapidus hopes to capitalise on. TSMC "will continue to dominate the majority of the market. But there are plenty of customers in the remaining 20% who cannot get capacity from TSMC because they are low on its priority list or their orders are small," said Akira Minamikawa, an analyst at Omdia. Rapidus CEO Atsuyoshi Koike expressed confidence there was enough market demand to support an additional leading-edge manufacturer. "One or two companies are nowhere near enough," Koike told Reuters. Some potential customers remain cautious. "We're already having TSMC make our chips, so we can't switch everything to Rapidus. If it didn't work out, we couldn't go back to TSMC, so we have to be cautious," said one executive who declined to be identified because the deliberations are private. Customers may use Rapidus to diversify supply chains, while the presence of a leading-edge manufacturer could also benefit Japan's materials and equipment makers, Minamikawa said. Japan's global semiconductor market share has fallen from about 50% in the 1980s to less than 10% today. Chipmakers operating in Japan include memory producer Kioxia (285A.T) . TSMC itself is also present through a partnership with Sony (6758.T) . Other government-backed initiatives include [USN:L1N43O03Q TEXT:"Noetra"], which is developing a foundational model for physical AI and robotics. Japan's industry ministry in April announced it had approved an [USN:L4N40U047 TEXT:"additional $4 billion"] in assistance to Rapidus, bringing total research and development support to $15 billion. TECHNOLOGICAL HURDLES REMAIN Preparations for mass production were progressing on schedule and the environment was better than envisioned when Rapidus was founded in 2022, CEO Koike said. Yet significant technological hurdles remain. Rapidus continues to work with IBM (IBM.N) and has started pilot operations, but experts said commercial success remains far from guaranteed. "Running a chip fab around the clock, maintaining stable, consistent yields and continuing production in a way that makes the business viable is extremely difficult," said Kazuyoshi Saito, an analyst at IwaiCosmo Securities. "Even Samsung ... has struggled." Beyond proving its technology, Rapidus faces the longer-term challenge of building a profitable business. The company has targeted an initial public offering for around the financial year ending March 2032. "Its success or failure won't be known for 10 years and no one will be able to take responsibility" if it is not a success, said a government official. Still, Rapidus' backers have ambitious plans. A listing and manufacturing operations in the United States are possibilities, said Daishiro Yamagiwa, a lawmaker who heads the ruling Liberal Democratic Party's parliamentary group on chip strategy.

item.title: US luxury spending slows ahead of midterms, credit card data shows
item.description: The data signals further weakness in the industry's biggest market as the US heads into the November 3 midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: US credit card spending on luxury brands fell for a third consecutive month in September, retail lender Citi said on Tuesday, signalling further weakness in the industry's biggest market as the US heads into the November 3 midterm elections . Buffeted by prolonged weakness in China and the economic fallout of the Iran war , luxury brands have pinned hopes on resilient demand from wealthy US shoppers, including a [USN:L6N42X136 TEXT:"growing cohort of AI millionaires"], to offset softer sales elsewhere and help lift the sector out of a prolonged downturn. While continued wealth growth among affluent consumers supported the top-end of the market in September, overall US luxury credit card purchases fell 6% from a year earlier, after declining 4% in both July and August, Citi analysts said in a research note. The luxury brands most exposed to the US include Tapestry (TPR.N) , owner of Coach and Kate Spade; French conglomerate LVMH (LVMH.PA) , known for brands like Louis Vuitton and Tiffany; and Italy's Ferragamo (SFER.MI) , they said. Still "brands with greater exposure to higher-end consumers should remain relatively resilient, supported by equity-market wealth effects," Citi said. Spending on leather goods and ready-to-wear items improved sequentially in September, the note added, while watches and luxury jewellery deteriorated even further. Most soft luxury brands which sell apparel, shoes and leather goods have raised their prices by low single digits in percentage terms so far this year, slightly below the low to mid-single-digit price increases from watch and jewellery makers, the note said. A COOLING ECONOMY The Citi data, based on millions of credit card transactions, follows surveys from the [USN:L1N45L0LX TEXT:"Conference Board"] and the [USN:L1N45G0ZD TEXT:"University of Michigan"] that showed growing unease about the US economy ahead of the midterm elections, when voters will decide control of Congress. The run-up to elections is often marked by heightened caution among consumers and businesses as political uncertainty weighs on spending decisions. [USN:L6N4560YU TEXT:"Economists say"] rising US Treasury yields and mortgage rates could further cool economic activity. Morgan Stanley analysts said in September that the downturn in US luxury spending leaves brands with little scope to deliver the long-awaited return to growth after two consecutive years of contraction. The brokerage expects luxury groups to flag weaker US demand during the upcoming earnings season, which begins on October 12 when LVMH, widely seen as a bellwether for the industry, reports third-quarter sales. Gucci owner Kering (PRTP.PA) , which releases earnings on October 22, told analysts last week to expect a slowdown in the US market, according to Italian brokerage Equita.

item.title: Samsung's Q3 profit seen jumping nine-fold, but chip margins may be flat
item.description: Samsung Electronics is expected to report a nearly nine-fold jump in third-quarter operating profit, driven by robust AI demand, though analysts have cut forecasts by nearly 8% since the end of August.
item.dc:creator: Hyunjoo Jin
item.content:encoded: Samsung Electronics is expected to report a nearly nine-fold jump in third-quarter operating profit, driven by robust AI demand, though analysts have cut forecasts by nearly 8% since the end of August. Despite moderating gains in the prices of memory chips and a strengthening South Korean won, the world's largest memory-chip maker is expected to post operating profit of 106.1 trillion won ($79.1 billion) for the July-September quarter. The LSEG SmartEstimate, based on forecasts from 21 analysts, and weighted toward those with stronger track records has been slashed by 7.7% since the end of August. It will be up from 12.17 trillion won a year earlier for Samsung's (005930.KS) fourth consecutive quarter of record operating profit, underscoring a prolonged memory shortage as demand for AI infrastructure outstrips supply growth. Chipmakers expect the shortage, which began more than a year ago, to persist into next year and perhaps through 2028. However, the pace of price increases slowed in the third quarter, fanning concerns that chip margins may have peaked and prompting questions about the durability of the AI spending boom. Samsung will provide preliminary Q3 results on Thursday before detailed data is released in late October. The moderation in memory prices is being closely watched by investors after a more than one-year-long rally fuelled by AI-driven demand. That rally propelled the world's largest memory producers Samsung, SK Hynix (000660.KS) and Micron (MU.O) , to record profits and margins. RISING COST BURDEN Higher chip prices have pushed up the cost of smartphones and consumer electronics, weighing on demand. At the same time, long-term supply deals between chipmakers and customers have limited price gains in exchange for guaranteed supply. TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter from the preceding quarter, slowing from a second-quarter surge of roughly 60%. "Although the market remains in a tight supply position, the pace of price growth is expected to decelerate," said Avril Wu, its senior vice president for research. Suppliers are wary of further steep price increases that could hurt demand across a broad range of consumer electronics, Wu added. "In addition, long-term agreements represent an increasingly higher proportion of suppliers' total output. With ceiling-price mechanisms built in, the rate of price increases has slowed down," Wu said. In July Samsung said it aimed to secure long-term contracts covering about two-thirds of its memory output, joining rivals seeking to reduce exposure to the industry's boom-and-bust cycles. US rival Micron [USN:L6N45M1AE TEXT:"said"] the chip market could be tighter in 2027 and 2028 than this year, although it expects its gross margin to slip to 86.3% in the current quarter, from 87%, partly due to employee compensation costs. Samsung's memory-chip operating profit margin is expected to reach 76% in the third quarter, flat with the preceding quarter, estimates by SK Securities analyst Han Dong-hee show. It also faces growing competition from Chinese rivals, which remain concentrated in lower-end products but are benefiting from the AI-driven memory shortage. "Our industry checks indicate that an increasing number of OEMs and ODMs are adopting Chinese DRAM and NAND," Kinngai Chan, senior research analyst at Summit Insights Group, said in a report. Currency swings are another headwind. The won strengthened 14.3% against the dollar in the third quarter, rebounding sharply from 17-year lows for its biggest quarterly gain since early 1998. That reduces the value of overseas earnings when repatriated. Samsung shares have fallen about 25% from a June record but remain more than double their level at the start of the year. The company is expected to boost sales of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, a critical component for AI data centres, as it narrows the gap with market leader SK Hynix. Samsung had lagged in HBM supplies after delays in qualifying products for Nvidia (NVDA.O) , but has gained ground this year by expanding shipments of its latest HBM4 chips. Its HBM market share is expected to rise to 34% this year from 20% last year, J.P. Morgan estimates, while SK Hynix's share is forecast to fall to 46% from 60%. ($1=1,341.7500 won)

item.title: In interview, US Vice President Vance says Iran must cut enrichment to end war
item.description: US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with Reuters that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ seven-month war.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Bogage
item.content:encoded: US Vice President JD Vance said in an exclusive interview with Reuters that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations. Vance, a longtime skeptic of US involvement in foreign wars, has [USN:L8N42P1PE TEXT:"taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement"] to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in June that quickly fell apart. The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections. Speaking on Monday after a campaign trip in Alaska, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns. "If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity." Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer and has warned that military operations could intensify after the midterms. Vance said the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions. "We're not going to trade words for actions," Vance said. UNCLEAR HOW IRAN MAKES DECISIONS: VANCE Complicating matters, Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran. Vance said the US was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran's power structure, he said, after joint US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. "One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his "[USN:S0N44P02O TEXT:"biggest problem"]" is no one knows who is running Iran. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that US officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran's decision-making system works. "The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials," Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference. Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions. He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway. Vance declined to say if he was leading peace talks, though he is frequently cited as the White House's top negotiator. "We're certainly involved," he said. "Ultimately, the president of the United States is driving things." The war — [USN:L6N4530XO TEXT:"and its $3 billion monthly price tag"] — has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress. Vance has sought to temper criticism of Trump’s handling of the conflict, telling voters they should not let that issue keep them from backing Republicans in next month's elections. In Alaska, [USN:L6N45R01A TEXT:"Vance rallied for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan"], who is locked in a tight reelection battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Trump carried Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but rising everyday costs have put the state in play. Before speaking with Reuters, Vance focused much of his speech on affordability concerns, especially around energy. Alaska's remote locale makes consumer goods more expensive, and energy production is a key industry. Rally attendees roared when Sullivan nearly introduced Vance as the president of the US, rather than the vice president. Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House. Vance told Reuters afterward that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028. "I'm inherently a procrastinator," he said. "I really haven't thought about it much."

item.title: North Korea criticises US support for Taiwan, pledges backing for Russia
item.description: North Korea criticised the United States over its arms sales and military support for Taiwan, accusing Washington of fuelling tension in the Taiwan Strait, state news agency KCNA said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Joyce Lee
item.content:encoded: North Korea criticised the United States over its arms sales and military support for Taiwan, accusing Washington of fuelling tension in the Taiwan Strait, state news agency KCNA said on Wednesday. A KCNA commentary citing North Korean international affairs analyst Kim Myong Chol said US policy on Taiwan was undermining peace and stability in the region and condemned the appearance of US-sold fighter aircraft in Taiwan. The US "should think twice whether it is ready to stand in frontal confrontation with the powerful national power of the People's Republic of China for the security of Taiwan and whether it can cope with its consequences," it added. [USN:L1N45O07H TEXT:"Last week"], Taiwan received the first two of a batch of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets ordered in 2019, in the face of a rising military threat from Beijing. The comments show Pyongyang is aligning more closely with China on Taiwan, one of Beijing's most sensitive foreign policy issues. China claims the democratically governed island as its own, though Taipei rejects the sovereignty assertion. North Korea has strengthened ties with China and Russia in recent years, raising security concerns for the US and its allies in Asia and the West. KIM OFFERED FULL SUPPORT AT JUNE SUMMIT North Korean leader Kim Jong Un told Chinese President Xi Jinping during a Pyongyang summit in June that he would [USN:L1N42G106 TEXT:"fully support"] the "One China" principle, which Beijing views as meaning that both sides of the Taiwan Strait belong to one country, regardless of changes in the international situation. The meeting also included a cautiously worded reference to defence links, with Xi saying both sides would enhance exchanges in diplomacy, law enforcement, military affairs and other fields, China's Foreign Ministry said. Analysts have said North Korea's decision to send soldiers to fight for Russia in the Ukraine war had shown it is willing to provide material assistance in wartime, but with no sign of a comparable commitment to China. China describes Taiwan as the "core of core issues" in its ties with other countries, demanding no form of official engagement between Taiwanese and foreign leaders. Taiwan's government says Beijing has no right to claim the island or try to represent it on the international stage. China, a treaty ally of North Korea, has also repeatedly demanded that Washington end arms sales to Taiwan. The United States is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Kim pledged continued support for Russia and its war effort in a birthday message to President Vladimir Putin, KCNA said in a separate report. Pyongyang would keep up joint work under their comprehensive strategic partnership, Kim said. He was convinced that Russia's "sacred war of justice" to defend its sovereignty, security interests and territorial integrity would end in victory, he added. The message did not explicitly mention Russia's war in Ukraine. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to [USN:L1N45K11J TEXT:"support Russia"] in the conflict since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates. North Korea and Russia have strengthened ties sharply since a mutual defence pact signed in June 2024.

item.title: Allemagne-Un ancien directeur du renseignement arrêté pour des soupçons de trahison
item.description: L'ancien chef du service allemand du renseignement extérieur (BND), August Hanning, a été arrêté mardi pour des soupçons de tentative de trahison, une affaire qui constitue l'un des plus importants scandales ayant éclaboussé les services des renseignements allemands depuis la Guerre froide.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'ancien chef du service allemand du renseignement extérieur (BND), August Hanning, a été arrêté mardi pour des soupçons de tentative de trahison, une affaire qui constitue l'un des plus importants scandales ayant éclaboussé les services des renseignements allemands depuis la Guerre froide. August Hanning est accusé par le parquet d'avoir payé pour se procurer des documents secrets après avoir quitté ses fonctions et d'avoir utilisé ces documents pour effectuer une analyse au bénéfice d'un service étranger du renseignement. Les procureurs n'ont pas précisé dans l'immédiat de quel service étranger il s'agissait ni si l'analyse en question a effectivement été transmise à son destinataire voulu. D'après le magazine d'information Der Spiegel, les enquêteurs étudient un possible lien avec l'Azerbaïdjan, alors qu'August Hanning aurait été en contact avec un agent de ce pays. Le parquet fédéral a décliné une demande de commentaire, de même que la chancellerie. Aucun commentaire n'a pu être obtenu auprès d'August Hanning. Jamais, auparavant, un ex-chef du service du renseignement extérieur n'avait été arrêté en Allemagne, dont les relations en matière de renseignements avec des pays alliés pourraient pâtir de cette affaire, a déclaré un élu sécuritaire de haut rang. Dans un communiqué, le parquet a déclaré qu'August Hanning était "fortement suspecté d'espionnage perfide, d'avoir obtenu des secrets d'Etat, de tentative de trahison et d'espionnage". Selon les procureurs, August Hanning était convenu avec le responsable de bureau du BND, cinq ans après son départ du service, dont il a occupé la présidence pendant sept ans jusqu'en 2005, de recevoir des renseignements confidentiels en échange de paiements. Ce responsable de bureau, identifié comme étant Manfred D., dans le respect des règles de confidentialité en Allemagne, a également été arrêté mardi. Les deux hommes devaient comparaître devant un juge de la Cour fédérale de justice. L'AFFAIRE NE CONCERNERAIT PAS LA RUSSIE Manfred D. a été responsable de bureau du BND pour plusieurs présidents successifs du service, jusqu'en mars dernier, ce qui lui a potentiellement permis d'accéder à certains renseignements toujours d'actualité au moment où, d'après les procureurs, des documents ont été "siphonnés" du BND. Quelque 2.000 documents auraient été fournis par Manfred D. au fil des années, ont dit les procureurs, ajoutant que parmi ces documents figuraient des éléments classifiés destinés uniquement à un usage interne au BND et à des compte-rendus auprès de représentants de haut rang à la chancellerie. Selon le journal Sueddeutsche Zeitung, les documents en question concernent le programme nucléaire iranien et l'armée russe, de même que des documents classés secrets transmis par des services de renseignement alliés à propos d'autres pays. Les procureurs accusent August Hanning d'avoir utilisé des informations classifiées transmises par Manfred D. pour préparer une analyse destinée à un officier d'un service étranger du renseignement et d'avoir pendant des années partagé des informations politiques avec un représentant de ce service. Cette affaire ne concerne pas la Russie, selon une information obtenue par le Sueddeutsche Zeitung. L'actuel président du BND a déclaré que le service a lancé une enquête interne approfondie dès que les premiers soupçons sont apparus. "Il ne peut y avoir aucun compromis sur la sécurité interne", a ajouté Martin Jäger.

item.title: Why have India-US trade talks stalled again and what's next?
item.description: Senior officials in India and the United States have indicated long-running efforts to finalise a bilateral trade agreement have stalled, again.
item.dc:creator: Shivangi Acharya, Manoj Kumar
item.content:encoded: Senior officials in India and the United States have indicated long-running efforts to finalise a bilateral trade agreement have stalled, again. Both nations had agreed to a [USN:L1N3YY0U1 TEXT:"framework for the deal"] in February which brought down to 18% [USN:L1N3UJ03Y TEXT:"from 50%"] the punitive tariff on most Indian goods imposed in August last year after a previous round of [USN:L4N3TT0LO TEXT:"talks collapsed"]. In the meantime, the Supreme Court invalidated US President Donald Trump's use of emergency powers to impose sweeping tariffs globally, leading to a 10% [USN:L1N3ZG0T5 TEXT:"baseline rate"]. But a final deal between two of the world's biggest economies remains elusive. WHY HAVE TRADE TALKS HIT A WALL? Trade talks have [USN:L1N45R03N TEXT:"reached a "plateau""] with little room for manoeuvre, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said earlier this week, following United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer's comment that a deal is [USN:S0N40K049 TEXT:"not "imminent"]." Neither side has detailed reasons for the delay in finalising the deal. But talks in the past months have met with complications, most recently [USN:L1N4590XN TEXT:"a new US law"] that paves the way for up to 100% tariffs on Indian goods because of New Delhi's purchase of Russian oil. Those purchases have not been significantly reduced. The potentially stiff levy goes against New Delhi's [USN:L4N42U08S TEXT:"efforts to secure"] tariff terms better than peer economies, including Vietnam and China. A deal has also been held back because Washington is [USN:L1N4290B6 TEXT:"yet to complete"] a Section 301 trade investigation on several nations over alleged excess industrial capacity. The probe is to evaluate whether such overproduction is hurting or undercutting American industries. Unless this probe is completed, it is hard to tell what final tariff Indian goods will attract. Overall, bilateral ties between India and the US have been rocky this past year, casting a shadow on [USN:L1N45904J TEXT:"efforts to stabilise"] their trade partnership. Events including a [USN:L1N42K089 TEXT:"US military attack"] on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers and [USN:L1N3TP08X TEXT:"India rejecting"] Trump's repeated claim of brokering a ceasefire with Pakistan have hurt relations. WHAT IS AT STAKE? The US is India's largest export market and exports have so far been [USN:L4N3XL16E TEXT:"resilient"]. India's goods exports to the United States rose to $42.79 billion in April-August from $40.39 billion a year earlier. In the fiscal year 2025/26, India enjoyed a nearly $34 billion trade surplus with the US. India says many of its largest export categories to the US, including generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones, are not subject to the current 10% levy. But analysts say that in the absence of a trade deal, India risks higher US tariffs from the ongoing trade probe and purchase of Russian oil, even if it could negotiate for waivers under the sanctions law. Another increase in tariffs could hurt businesses, dent market sentiment and hurt the Indian currency, which is already trading close to record lows. WHAT MORE DO THE TWO SIDES WANT? India is striving to protect politically sensitive sectors, particularly agriculture, while securing [USN:L1N43F08Q TEXT:"better tariff treatment"] for its exporters. India has sought to keep dairy, poultry, rice, wheat and other farm products outside the scope of market-opening commitments. It wants greater certainty over US tariffs before making concessions. The Trump administration wants India to cut Russian oil purchases, arguing Indian purchases of Russian crude help finance the war in Ukraine. India says decisions on where to source fuel are driven by [USN:L4N45A0SX TEXT:"the energy needs"] of its 1.4-billion-strong population. Russian crude became particularly important after Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine because it was available at discounted prices. The war in the Middle East and resulting disruptions have sharpened the calculation over energy imports. ARE FURTHER TALKS PLANNED? US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to visit India later this month, when two-way talks could make some progress. Modi and Trump, who spoke by phone on September 30, are also expected to speak again soon to review progress. Modi is expected to visit the US in December for a G20 leaders' meet.

item.title: Planned Moldova-Romania power line to be named after Trump
item.description: A planned high-voltage power line linking Romania and Moldova will be named the "Trump Liberty Line," the US embassy in Chisinau said on Monday, making it the latest infrastructure project to bear the name of US President Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A planned high-voltage power line linking Romania and Moldova will be named the "Trump Liberty Line," the US embassy in Chisinau said on Monday, making it the latest infrastructure project to bear the name of US President Donald Trump. The embassy said in a post on X that the project, "backed by a $130 million US government investment", would strengthen Moldova's energy security and independence "The Government of the Republic of Moldova supports initiatives that benefit the citizens of the Republic of Moldova, especially those that ensure the country's security and energy infrastructure," government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici told Reuters "The Romanian government has always supported interconnecting projects between Romania and Moldova, and the fact the United States supports and finances them only reconfirms their strategic importance," said government spokeswoman Ioana Dogioiu. Moldova, one of Europe's poorest countries and a candidate for European Union membership, imports most of its electricity via existing links with Romania and Ukraine. Russian attacks on Ukraine's power infrastructure have disrupted those supplies in the past Trump's name has been attached to a growing number of projects around the world, including a proposed transport corridor through Armenia and a planned military base in Poland, as governments seek to win favour with the US president

item.title: For Trump’s Treasury, the sting is in the auction ‘tail’
item.description: US Treasury auctions are supposed to be dull, predictable, and non-newsworthy affairs. But these are not normal times, and the Trump administration now risks seeing weak debt sales make headline news.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: US Treasury auctions are supposed to be dull, predictable, and non-newsworthy affairs. But these are not normal times, and the Trump administration now risks seeing weak debt sales make headline news. The Treasury plans to sell nearly $120 billion of debt this week, the first sales outside of T-bills in two weeks: $58 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday, $39 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday, and $22 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday. These might normally be non-events, but they're under increasing scrutiny because the September 22-24 auctions were remarkably weak, particularly the five-year note auction on Sept. 23, which helped spark the biggest rise in bond yields since April last year. Yields have not come down since and have instead powered ahead to multi-decade highs across most maturities. It's worth stating that there's next to zero chance that the US would ever have a "failed" debt auction. Primary dealers – the 26 Wall Street banks and institutions currently approved by the New York Fed as Treasury market makers – will always participate. They effectively underwrite the sales, ensuring the $30 trillion US debt market – the most liquid market in the world – functions smoothly. This, in turn, keeps the entire global financial system chugging along, as well. Trillions of dollars of global debt, assets, and market derivatives use Treasuries as a reference. US government bonds are also the collateral used to lubricate the pipes of US and global financial plumbing - repo agreements, interbank lending, and funding. In short, as long as US debt is the lynchpin of the global financial system, there will always be buyers at Treasury auctions. The issue, as ever, is the price at which these sales clear. Right now, borrowing costs on the secondary market are the highest since the mid to early 2000s, so it is reasonable to assume that Treasury will pay comparably high rates on the primary market. But as the most recent auctions have shown, there is also still room for negative surprises. TOO BIG TO TAIL? The $70 billion sale of five-year notes on September 23 was one of the most alarming in recent memory. Demand as measured by the 'bid-to-cover' ratio was the lowest in nine years. Treasury ultimately sold the notes at 5.033%, which was more than three basis points above the market yield at the bidding deadline. Three basis points might not sound like a lot, but for a five-year auction, that’s extraordinary. It was the largest so-called "tail" since June 2022. To find the last time a five-year auction had a 3 bps "tail," JP Morgan analysts note, you have to go all the way back to 2011, when a brewing debt ceiling crisis would lead to a credit rating downgrade that August. Moving back to the present, concerns about the dire US fiscal outlook have pushed up long-term borrowing costs. As a result, the Trump administration is widely expected to gradually shift the weight of the Treasury’s huge borrowing requirements towards the shorter - and cheaper - end of the curve. This is why the five-year auction two weeks ago caused such alarm. "Tails" of 3 bps are common in longer bond auctions, but not in sales of debt that sit right in the so-called "belly" of the yield curve. If Treasury is being forced to pay higher premiums to shift these notes, then Houston, we have a problem. Fat auction “tails” can be a result of multiple forces, including market volatility on the day itself or more worrying fundamental issues that might erode demand over time. It's often difficult to untangle the two dynamics, as they are not mutually exclusive. On a more optimistic note, these jitters haven’t migrated to the front end of the curve. Yet. Three-year and 10-year yields are up around 50 basis points from their last auctions a month ago, hovering around 4.96% and 5.32%, respectively. The 30-year yield is up around 35 bps at 5.65%. That should be high enough to attract solid demand and ensure smooth sales, right? Probably. But if there’s a sting in the tails, volatility and uncertainty could bite across the market. Investors will be watching like, well, hawks. (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column?
